title: Merged: VIP:::FRCS:DKA: Systemic Emergency & Ophthalmic Implications
summary: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a life-threatening triad of hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. While primarily systemic, it presents critical ophthalmic risks including acute refractive shifts, snowflake cataracts, and the vision-threatening emergency of Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis.

branches: Ketosis: Presence of Acetoacetate/β-hydroxybutyrate in blood or urine
Metabolic Acidosis: Arterial pH <7.30 or Bicarbonate <18 mEq/L

rows: Osmotic swelling of the lens and changes in aqueous refractive index.
Subcapsular opacities due to sudden osmotic stress; may be reversible with slow control.
Severe dehydration leading to decreased aqueous production by ciliary body.
Can occur due to cranial nerve palsies or secondary Mucormycosis.
Secondary to invasive fungal infections (Mucor/Rhizopus) in acidotic states.
Creamy white appearance of retinal vessels when serum triglycerides >2500 mg/dL.

sections.title: CRITICAL EMERGENCY: Mucormycosis
content: Rhino-orbital-cerebral Mucormycosis is a fatal fungal infection triggered by DKA.
Red Flag: Black necrotic eschar on the palate or turbinates.
Red Flag: Orbital Apex Syndrome (CN III, IV, VI, V1 involvement) + Vision Loss.
Mechanism: Acidosis releases iron from sequestering proteins, feeding fungal growth (Rhizopus/Mucor).
Treatment: URGENT surgical debridement + IV Amphotericin B + Reversal of Acidosis.

sections.title: Systemic Pathophysiology
content: 1. Absolute Insulin Deficiency + Counter-regulatory Hormone Excess (Glucagon, Cortisol).
2. Increased Lipolysis → Increased Free Fatty Acids.
3. Hepatic Ketogenesis → Production of Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate.
4. Ketoacidosis → Bicarbonate buffering exhaustion.
5. Osmotic Diuresis → Profound dehydration and electrolyte depletion (K+, Na+).

sections.title: Stepwise Management Protocol
content: 1. Fluid Resuscitation: 1L 0.9% NaCl over 1 hour, then adjust based on Na+ status.
2. Potassium Replacement: If K+ <5.2 mEq/L, start replacement BEFORE or with insulin. If K+ <3.3, hold insulin.
3. Insulin Therapy: 0.1 Unit/kg bolus followed by 0.1 U/kg/hr infusion. Goal: Reduce glucose by 50-75 mg/dL/hr.
4. Glucose Switch: When blood glucose reaches 200 mg/dL, add 5% Dextrose (D5NS) to prevent hypoglycemia.
5. Bicarbonate: Only if pH <6.9. Rarely used due to risk of paradoxical CSF acidosis.

content.explanation: D: Dehydration (Isotonic Saline); K: Potassium (Replace even if normal due to total body depletion); A: Anion Gap (Target the gap, not just the glucose).

rows: History of binge, lower glucose levels

sections.title: Ocular Investigation & Imaging
content: Dilated Fundus Exam: Monitor for progression of DR after rapid glycemic control (Early Worsening Phenomenon).
CT/MRI Orbit & Sinuses: Indicated if any ptosis, proptosis, or ophthalmoplegia (Rule out Mucor).
A-Scan/B-Scan: Evaluate lens thickness and vitreous status if view is obscured.
IOP Measurement: High importance as hypotony reflects systemic hydration status.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Pseudohyponatremia: Measured Na+ drops 1.6 mEq/L for every 100 mg/dL glucose elevation.
Paradoxical DR Worsening: Aggressive insulin therapy can temporarily exacerbate Diabetic Retinopathy.
Euglycemic DKA: Seen in patients on SGLT2 inhibitors (Canagliflozin); pH is low but glucose is <250.
Cerebral Edema: Most common cause of death in pediatric DKA patients; monitor for headache and bradycardia.

sections.title: Recent Landmark Studies
sections.content: The DCCT (Diabetic Control and Complications Trial) and EDIC follow-up studies established the 'Metabolic Memory' concept. While intensive control prevents long-term DR, rapid correction in the setting of DKA/severe hyperglycemia can lead to transient worsening of soft exudates and macular edema. The CLOVER trial and various ADA guidelines emphasize that managing DKA requires focusing on the anion gap closure rather than just normalization of blood glucose.
